title: Canaries, Interest Rates, and Timing: More on the Recent Drivers of Employment Changes for Young Workers
author: Erik Brynjolfsson · Bharat Chandar · Ruyu Chen

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s account of unsettled labour effects by refining the estimated onset of the entry-level decline to 2024 under firm-time controls, weakening interest rates as an alternative explanation, and documenting a growing, unreversed decline through October 2025. Its qualifications reinforce the cluster’s caution against treating these findings as universal or definitively causal.
qs: - On the timing, we do find suggestive evidence that when you include the broadest set of controls (firm-time fixed-effects), the timing of the employment decline in AI-exposed occupations becomes significant only in 2024; the earlier declines are likely (at least partly) due to some combination of other factors, not just AI.

With the fixed-effect approach, the employment changes start later, but they are growing (reaching about 16% by October 2025, vs 13% in our paper with data only through July), and they have not shown a reversal.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between observed early-career employment declines and causal attribution to AI. It finds larger declines in highly AI-exposed occupations even across interest-rate exposure groups, while emphasizing that contemporaneous factors, measurement limits and stronger controls prevent treating AI as the sole established cause.
qs: In both cases we found that the most AI-exposed occupations (darkest shade of gray) have greater declines in employment than the average occupation (red).

As we noted in our November paper, and we now want to re-emphasize: we do not believe that AI is always and everywhere the sole determinant of employment, and we do not encourage others to interpret our results in that way.

st.t: Entry routes: Reduced hiring precedes broader displacement
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by documenting a growing relative employment decline among highly AI-exposed workers aged 22–25, while showing that stronger firm-time controls shift its notable onset to 2024. It also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that the association is suggestive rather than causal and may reflect multiple contemporaneous factors.
qs: In our regression analysis with firm-time effects, we find a relative decline in employment for the most-exposed young workers (quintile 5, and to some extent quintile 4 in Figure 3) that starts becoming notable in 2024 (not late 2022 or 2023 as in Figure 2).

kp.k: Interest rates poorly explain AI-exposed entry-level employment declines
kp.d: In this 2026 note revisiting their paper last revised November 13, 2025, Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen argue that existing evidence does not strongly support interest rate changes as an explanation for disproportionate entry-level employment declines in AI-exposed occupations. This is a cross-occupational labor-market finding, not a finding specifically about legal employment; the authors acknowledge that interest rates affect overall employment.
qs: Looking at the totality of the existing evidence, we do not find strong support for the hypothesis that interest rate changes explain the disproportionate decline in entry-level employment for AI-exposed occupations that we uncovered.

kp.k: AI exposure correlates negatively with interest rate sensitivity
kp.d: Combining occupational interest rate sensitivity estimates shared by Zens et al. (2020) with AI exposure measures from Eloundou et al. (2024), the authors find that more AI-exposed jobs are less interest-rate-exposed on average. Construction illustrates the opposite combination: high interest rate exposure and low AI exposure. Within both above-median and below-median interest-rate-exposure groups, the most AI-exposed occupations exhibit larger early-career employment declines than the average occupation.
qs: Figure 1: The sensitivity of occupational employment to interest rates is negatively correlated to AI-exposure.
For example, occupations such as construction have high interest rate exposure and low AI exposure.
In both cases we found that the most AI-exposed occupations (darkest shade of gray) have greater declines in employment than the average occupation (red).

kp.k: Interest rate evidence lacks occupational and age granularity
kp.d: The authors qualify their interest rate comparison because the interest rate data are less occupationally granular than the AI exposure data, and the Zens et al. estimates do not condition on age. Young workers could have different occupational interest rate exposure from the workforce overall, leaving the interest rate channel open to further testing.
qs: First, the available interest rate data do not have as much occupational granularity as the AI exposure data from Eloundou et al. (2024).
Second, the Zens et al. (2020) estimates do not condition on age, and young workers may potentially have different occupational interest rate exposure than the workforce as a whole.

kp.k: Firm-time controls shift employment decline onset to 2024
kp.d: Regressions controlling for overall changes in firm employment place the onset of the relative employment decline in 2024 rather than late 2022 or 2023. The event study concerns workers aged 22 to 25, with declines most apparent in AI-exposure quintile 5 and to some extent quintile 4. The authors interpret this timing shift as suggesting that earlier declines were at least partly attributable to factors other than AI.
qs: Specifically, one way to get a sense of the role of other macroeconomic factors compared to AI is to consider our results that control for overall changes in firm employment.

In our regression analysis with firm-time effects, we find a relative decline in employment for the most-exposed young workers (quintile 5, and to some extent quintile 4 in Figure 3) that starts becoming notable in 2024 (not late 2022 or 2023 as in Figure 2).
Figure 3: Event study estimates for employment changes by AI exposure for workers aged 22 to 25. Controlling for firm-time effects.

kp.k: Estimated decline grows to about 16% by October 2025
kp.d: Under the fixed-effect approach, the authors report that employment changes start later but grow to about 16% by October 2025, compared with 13% in their paper using data only through July. They report no reversal and recommend close monitoring; these figures describe the reported relative employment decline, not an experimentally established AI displacement effect.
qs: With the fixed-effect approach, the employment changes start later, but they are growing (reaching about 16% by October 2025, vs 13% in our paper with data only through July), and they have not shown a reversal.
Given these trends, these employment changes bear close monitoring.

kp.k: Employment associations do not establish AI as sole cause
kp.d: The authors explicitly reject interpreting AI as the sole determinant of employment and describe the sharp decline among young software developers as having multiple causes. Divergence after ChatGPT's release could reflect contemporaneous changes rather than AI alone. Without an experiment comparing worlds with and without AI, they frame causal interpretation as an ongoing research question rather than a settled finding.
qs: While these charts are suggestive of a relationship between AI and employment, we can't be sure of the causality from this sort of analysis.
For example, the precipitous decline in employment for young software developers is a consequence of various factors.
Even if employment outcomes diverge notably only after the release of ChatGPT, this could be driven by other changes that occurred at the same time.
Since we don't have an experiment where we can compare a world with AI to one without, this will remain an active area for scientific research and discussion.

kp.k: Different methods and continued monitoring remain necessary
kp.d: The authors encourage consideration of other studies of AI's broad employment effects because different datasets and methods have different strengths and weaknesses. They commit to periodic updates to determine whether the identified trends persist, strengthen, reverse or otherwise change, rather than predicting their inevitable continuation.
qs: By now, there are several papers exploring the broad employment effects of AI, each using different data and methods, and thus subject to different strengths and weaknesses.
We will be actively monitoring the labor market and updating our results periodically to see if the trends we identified persist, strengthen, reverse, or change in some other ways.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen report a disproportionate relative employment decline among young workers in highly AI-exposed occupations, while rejecting an exclusively AI-driven interpretation.
pts.d: This cross-domain source concerns employment, not legal services specifically. The authors argue that existing evidence does not strongly support interest-rate changes as an explanation for the disproportionate decline in entry-level employment in AI-exposed occupations. With firm-time fixed effects, the relationship becomes notable in 2024 and the relative decline reaches about 16% by October 2025, compared with 13% in the paper using data through July. They report no reversal but do not predict that the trend must continue or claim to establish AI causation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors offer occupational exposure comparisons, employment trajectories and a firm-time fixed-effects event study as observational evidence.
pts.d: The note builds on their 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' paper, last revised November 13, 2025. Combining interest-rate exposure data shared by Zens et al. (2020) with AI exposure from Eloundou et al. (2024), they report a negative correlation between the two exposure measures. In occupations both above and below median interest-rate exposure, the most AI-exposed occupations show larger early-career employment declines than the average occupation. Their regression controls for overall changes in firm employment. They qualify the interest-rate comparison because its occupational categories are less granular and its estimates do not condition on age; young workers' exposure may differ from that of the overall workforce. The supplied text describes the figures but does not provide underlying observations or detailed statistical estimates.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The controlled relationship emerges in 2024 rather than late 2022 or 2023; the reported decline extends through October 2025, with future direction explicitly uncertain.
pts.d: In this 2026 note, the authors distinguish earlier descriptive declines from the later relationship observed after including firm-time fixed effects. They describe the controlled decline as becoming significant in 2024, although one passage says 'only after 2024'; the specific regression discussion and conclusion place its onset in 2024. Earlier declines likely reflect other factors at least partly, and temporal proximity to ChatGPT's release does not establish causation. The authors propose continued monitoring rather than a definite forecast of further displacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected group is early-career workers, specifically ages 22–25 in the event study, in occupations with the greatest AI exposure.
pts.d: The authors locate the controlled relative employment decline primarily in the highest AI-exposure quintile and to some extent in the fourth quintile. They describe disproportionate declines in entry-level hiring and employment, without separately quantifying hiring flows in the supplied text. Young software developers are an example of a group experiencing a sharp employment decline that the authors attribute to multiple factors, not AI alone. Construction illustrates high interest-rate exposure but low AI exposure. No distinct claims are made about lawyers, law firms or legal-services clients.
